newsitem.title: USA: CompuServe trims loss in latest quarter.
newsitem.headline: CompuServe trims loss in latest quarter.

text.p: CompuServe Corp. reported a slightly lower-than-expected quarterly loss Thursday, easing fears raised by the resignation three days earlier of the struggling online service's chief executive.

The world's No. 2 online service -- whose $14.2 million loss accounted for nearly half of the red ink posted by majority owner H&R Block Inc. in a separate earnings report -- said its overall membership continued to decline despite improvement in some areas.
Columbus, Ohio-based CompuServe said it would focus on returning to profitability by cutting costs and realigning its business structure.

The loss for the pioneering online service's third quarter ended Jan. 31, equivalent to 15 cents a share, compared with a profit of $17.2 million, or 13 cents a share in the year-ago quarter. Revenues rose to $211 million from $203 million.

Some analysts had feared the resignation Monday of Chief Executive Officer Robert Massey could signal more bad financial news. Industry analysts on average had expected a loss of 16 cents a share, according to the First Call service.
CompuServe stock rose 25 cents to $10.75 on Nasdaq.
The company's loss was a drag on the bottom line of H&R Block, the top U.S. tax preparation service and 80.1 percent owner of CompuServe.

The Kansas City, Mo.-based company -- which spun off 19.1 percent of CompuServe last April -- said the online service's loss accounted for $11.4 million of its total $25.3 million in losses for its third quarter.

"Returning CompuServe to profitability is our No. 1 goal," H&R Block Chief Executive Frank Salizzoni, also chairman and acting chief executive of CompuServe, said in a statement reporting H&R Block's results.
"While our third-quarter results show improvement over the second quarter, they are clearly not good enough," Salizzoni said in CompuServe's earnings report.
In the second quarter, CompuServe recorded a loss of $58 million, or 63 cents a share, including special charges, on $214 million in revenues.
Salizzoni is acting as CEO while CompuServe seeks a replacement for Massey.
CompuServe said it will continue to invest in its commercial networking business, which has been successful.
In the third quarter, Network Services added 90 corporate customers, compared with 52 in the second quarter. CompuServe now has 1,151 customers for data communications and other corporate services.
Prudential Securities analyst Lisa Thompson said revenues were "a little bit light," mostly because of a decline in membership in CompuServe's flagship CSi online service.

CompuServe said CSi membership dropped 100,000 to 2.8 million by the end of the quarter, with most of the decline coming from the United States. The number of U.S. subscribers fell 140,000 to 1.6 million.
In Europe, the number of subscribers to CSi rose 54,000 to 873,000 during the quarter. Subscribers from other overseas areas fell 14,000 to 365,000.
CompuServe's Internet-only access service, Sprynet, grew to 270,000 members from 218,000 in the second quarter.

Members for the combined CSi online service and Sprynet totalled 3.16 million in the third quarter, down from 3.31 million in the second quarter. CompuServe's exit from its flat-rate Wow! service for consumers and families accounted for 102,000 of the 150,000-member decline in CSi and Sprynet subscribers.

Including CompuServe's Japanese licensee, Nifty, CompuServe's total subscribers remained flat at 5.34 million in the third quarter. That ranks it second in the online industry behind America Online Inc., which has 8 million members.
Nesbitt Burns Securities analyst Abhishek Gami said the number of subscribers fell because the company spent less on marketing due to its exit from Wow!.
Thompson said she was encouraged by the company's strategy of aiming its flagship service at professional and business users and technical enthusiasts.

She also saw a silver lining in the company's withdrawal from Wow!, which left it as the only major online service not offering a flat rate for unlimited access. "As a result, they can actually pay (information) content people and have things that others don't have," she said.
